# Experimental Apple decoder

Remora's explicit `apple` VNC mode implements one plaintext Apple RFB 003.889 profile. Standard mode remains the default. Apple mode requires security type 30 (ARD), an extended shared ServerInit without session selection, 32-bit RGB888 pixels, and initialized pixels for each partial-update region. It advertises MVS encoding 1011, Raw, DesktopSize, DisplayInfo and DisplayInfo2. DisplayInfo2 and DesktopSize may change framebuffer geometry. Unsupported profiles and invalid geometry end the attempt. There is no alternate authentication retry, whole-session encryption, virtual display, media, HEVC, clipboard synchronization or dynamic resizing. The only reconnection is the same-profile transport recovery described under Connection reliability.

`mvs.c` and `mvs.h` derive from the v3 C port of [noVNC-ARD](https://github.com/peetinc/noVNC-ARD/tree/d699293635083c9e0c30c8f9480993865653772a/ard/decoders), revision `d699293635083c9e0c30c8f9480993865653772a`. The port covers full, partial, cache, match and quantization updates. The transform and entropy-decoding algorithms are unchanged. Remora adds per-pixel initialization masks to tile descriptors, rejects partial updates and match copies that read uninitialized pixels, and resets picture descriptors at display acknowledgements. Raw writes establish pixel coverage without creating or changing MVS differential descriptors. The stream cache and quantizers survive picture resets. The originals had SHA-256 `7efd6151967b4bb1313f8f849cbd284663a5554542c8e459e144d0a470cd87fd` (C) and `2da0cf4349d12f2ed8289e399a230c011a7b609ed7299d3bec33f7c4e6f08c45` (header). The MPL-2.0 license is in `../licenses/Apple-MVS-MPL-2.0.txt`. The IDCT attribution and IJG notices are retained. New adapter code is GPL-3.0-or-later.

The reference JavaScript wraps IDCT intermediate arithmetic to 32 bits. This C port computes the transform in 64 bits with the documented 32-bit workspace. Independent valid-stream comparisons found differences when dequantized coefficient magnitudes reached 32768 or greater. Apple's behavior in that range is unverified. Partial-state accumulation prevents assuming that real content cannot reach it. No overflow emulation is added here. Cache slots 1 through 64999 are supported and wrap to 1. Index 65000 always ends the session with a typed error, including cache-next after 64999. The JavaScript reference accepts this unwritten slot after 65000 inserts and reads past its typed array. Remora does not reproduce that behavior; Apple encoder/viewer behavior at that index is unknown. Full agreement with Apple's decoder remains unproven. Real-host validation is limited to the LAN measurements and editing workload below. The controlled Apple-viewer oracle covered only F0 and F1; its rejected F2 image was deleted and F3-F6 were not evaluated.

`apple.c` owns the private profile state. It parses bounded control bodies, limits compressed rectangles to the smaller of 64 MiB and `4 * rectangle area + 65536`, and accepts only aligned, framebuffer-contained MVS rectangles. The existing renderer limits remain 16384 pixels per axis and 67,108,864 pixels total. A malformed rectangle ends the session. There is no recovery using a partially consumed payload or a decoder that has failed.

Whole updates commit only after all rectangles validate. The adapter accumulates one bounding box from the decoder's existing written-tile callbacks and Raw rectangles, then publishes it once at the end of the message. DCT writes, cache loads and match copies contribute only their destination pixels, clipped at the framebuffer edge. Skipped tiles, skipped matches and quantization updates add no damage. A full MVS update contributes its actual written region. Full updates may initialize separate displays in separate messages, with unused space between them. A partial update requires initialized pixels only in its own region, and DCT deltas also require valid coefficient descriptors. The session bridge publishes the first selected picture only after all selected pixels are initialized. It reports that selected geometry before delivering the picture, then marks the selection ready. One bounding box uses constant storage and preserves the existing single-rectangle renderer path. Distant writes can include unchanged pixels between them. No callback exposes an incomplete message, even if the decoder wrote pixels before detecting its error.

The adapter sends shared ClientInit `0x81` and control SetMode 1 before the initial full FramebufferUpdateRequest. It then enables full-region, zero-interval AutoFBUpdate (`0x09`) before waiting for a baseline. While visible and awaiting a complete baseline, the worker retries a full, non-incremental request once per second between messages. Controls and incomplete coverage do not reset that retry interval. Partial MVS frames require complete initialization of their own region. It sends no automatic type-3 request per pushed update. Hidden demand pauses retries and sends AutoFBUpdate interval `0xffffffff`; resume sends interval 0 and preserves the existing immediate full-refresh request. Both subscription messages use header flags 1. Repeated demand does not generate refreshes. Closing the transport ends the subscription.

These startup and pause records follow the arm64e ScreenSharing framework and AppleVNCServer installed with macOS 27.0.1 (26A434). ScreenSharing's `stRequestUpdates` sends `RFBCheckForUpdate(ref, 1, NULL)` at `0x1cc068044`, then calls `stSetFrameUpdateInterval` at `0x1cc068214` before receiving a frame. `stSetFrameUpdateInterval` passes AutoFBUpdate flags 1 and maps a negative interval to `0xffffffff` at `0x1cc0daf18`. AppleVNCServer's `HandleAutoFrameBufferUpdateMessage` at `0x10001708c` enables automatic updates exactly when the interval differs from `0xffffffff`. SetMode 0 observes, SetMode 1 controls, and SetMode 2 inhibits local physical input when the server permits it. SetMode does not select a frame rate; Remora uses SetMode 1.

Server messages ARDAck (`0x04`), NOP (`0x07`) and StateChange (`0x14`) are handled in this profile. DisplayInfo2 (`0x51`) is also handled on standard RFB connections to Macs. Basic and Apple pasteboard bodies are discarded in chunks of at most 4096 bytes, with a 1 MiB body limit. Unknown messages and unsupported rectangle encodings fail closed.

Key and pointer events use the source-defined combined type `0x10`, flag 0 and a 16-byte AES-128-ECB block. Key-only blocks contain marker 255, direction and BE32 keysym in bytes 0 through 5. Pointer-only blocks contain marker 255, the button mask and BE16 coordinates in bytes 10 through 15. The unused half stays zero. Both kinds share the elapsed monotonic microseconds in bytes 6 through 9, modulo 2^32. The previous timestamp starts at zero, matching Screen Sharing, so the first event carries the low 32 bits of uptime. Flag 0 leaves the click count unspecified. This is Screen Sharing's 18-byte fallback; it requires no shared timebase. Only the ARD-derived 16-byte MD5 shared-secret key is retained after successful authentication. OpenSSL performs AES. Native state, key and block buffers are cleansed on failure, reinitialization and worker cleanup. No key enters Swift or diagnostics. The desktop transport remains unencrypted. The normal security selector still prefers VeNCrypt, but this Apple profile ends if the selected method is not ARD because no supported event key exists.

Option maps to Meta, legacy character keysyms above Latin-1 map to Unicode, and right/middle button bits swap at the Apple wire boundary. Source ownership stays in the existing input worker. Discrete scrolling follows ard-rs revision `7ff47199541c364cbba16e29c4410e39898ece0e`, `crates/ard-core/src/protocol.rs:917` and `crates/ard-viewer/src/session_runtime.rs:2058`. Positive native horizontal deltas correspond to RFB left (0x20); Remora right (0x40) becomes negative. Discrete scrolling uses the source-defined type `0x17`, subtype 11 record with line, 16.16 and point deltas, the event position, and the existing held-button mask. A local system arrow is explicitly emitted; unsupported remote cursor-shape encodings are not advertised.

`../patches/libvncclient-apple.patch` connects this module to the pinned LibVNCClient. It adds Apple display metadata to standard-mode parsing and refuses generic reported multi-display layouts without a selection protocol. Authentication selection is unchanged. `../build-vnc.sh` compiles this decoder in the Release engine with `-O3`, using the existing OpenSSL archive. `mise run test:mvs` runs `../tests/test-apple-mvs.sh`: the owned vectors, a golden hash over generated update sequences, a second hash over 300 valid pairs of a full update and the partial update that refines it, and bounded fuzz cases, under ASan/UBSan. Each hash covers every update's result, statistics, written rectangles and pixels, so a faster decoder must reproduce the current output bit for bit. `../tests/test-apple-mvs.sh bench` times generated partial updates of a 3024x1964 screen with the Release flags and no sanitizers. `python3 Vendor/tests/test-apple-session.py` drives the sanitized adapter and decoder through the public native API with an independently authenticated loopback peer. Swift public-session tests exercise the same wire framing and independent CommonCrypto key-event decryption. None of these tests establish Apple-viewer fidelity or real-host usability.

## Display selection and protocol evidence

The session lists physical displays from DisplayInfo2 and selects exactly one with SetDisplay (`0x0d`): `[type][combineAll=0][two zero bytes][BE32 display ID]`. There is no combined-display operation in the session API. Startup chooses the remotely flagged main display; if none is flagged, it chooses the first entry ordered by desktop x, y and display ID. Apple entry flag bit 0 identifies the main display. Desktop positions and framebuffer bounds are distinct; the session exposes desktop positions and physical pixel sizes.

DisplayInfo2 arrives as pseudo-encoding 1105 or server message `0x51`. Both carriers have a BE16 body length. The body contains a 20-byte header and 56 bytes per display. The parser accepts 1 through 64 entries, requires the exact declared length, rejects duplicate or reserved IDs, and validates pixel dimensions before allocation. Header pixel width and height determine selected framebuffer geometry, including a switch between equally sized displays. DisplayInfo 1101 is bounded and consumed for compatibility; it does not replace DisplayInfo2's main flag or geometry.

A 2026-11-13 native bridge probe against macOS 26.6.2 verified both Apple 003.889 and standard RFB 3.8. That server emitted DisplayInfo2 only when both 1101 and 1105 were advertised. It reported display 2 as main, 5120x2880 at desktop (0,0), and display 1 as 3024x1964 at (-1512,1440). Each dialect completed main 2 -> display 1 -> display 2 in one connection. Each transition delivered one fully initialized, nonblack picture at 5120x2880, 3024x1964 and 5120x2880, respectively, with native error 0. The probe sent no keyboard or pointer events and changed no remote display settings. Its private numeric receipts remain under `.snap/display-probe/` in the implementation worktree.

The standard Mac path keeps standard authentication and input framing. It requests lossless ZRLE/Raw, sends control SetMode 1, subscribes to AutoFBUpdate, and retries a full non-incremental request once per second while coverage is incomplete. The tested server initially sent only changed subrectangles after some selections; a later full request produced the missing complete picture. Display acknowledgements request a fresh picture and renew the subscription at the selected size. The client does not switch to Apple 003.889 to obtain this behavior. Standard mode retains its existing policy of continuing updates while hidden; Apple mode can pause its subscription.

An admitted switch clears readiness immediately. The worker cancels queued input and receipts, releases held input before SetDisplay, and resets its pointer state. It discards publication of in-flight old pictures. A matching DisplayInfo2 acknowledgement resets pixel and DCT coverage even when the dimensions are unchanged. Pixels reach FrameSink only after every selected pixel is initialized and every rectangle in the message validates. Input remains blocked until that picture is delivered. A switch has a ten-second bound that acknowledgements cannot extend; failure reports `DisplaySelectionFailure.timedOut` and leaves input and captures blocked until a successful retry. If the selected ID disappears, the session selects the remaining main display or deterministic first display. A new connection starts with a fresh inventory and the same startup policy; no display preference is saved.

Ordinary single-framebuffer VNC servers remain supported. Generic multi-display selection through ExtendedDesktopSize is not implemented. An applied ExtendedDesktopSize layout with more than one screen, without Apple display-selection metadata, ends the session with native error 12 before decoding subsequent combined pixel rectangles. A server that never reports its physical layout can only be treated as one framebuffer; Remora cannot discover unreported physical displays. No generic multi-screen selection or combined-display fallback is claimed.

Owned decoder and sanitized adapter tests initialize separate regions, accept partial updates inside initialized regions, and reject partial skips or DCT updates in untouched regions. Raw coverage tests include partial tiles and same-size picture resets. Public session fixtures cover both metadata carriers, remote-main startup, same-size switches with in-flight old pixels, input release before selection, incomplete-picture timeout and retry, and selection after unplug. These tests do not establish pixel fidelity against Apple's viewer or physical hot-unplug behavior on every server release. Physical hot-unplug and live input targeting were not performed during this display-selection probe.

## Responsiveness on LAN

On 2026-11-13, a development build on a MacBook Pro M4 Pro running macOS 27.0.1 was compared with Screen Sharing's standard connection using Adaptive Quality against a MacBook Pro M3 Pro running macOS 26.6.2 over Ethernet. Both clients showed the same 3024x1964 desktop in a 1512x1034 window. A local probe posted physical input and timed the first changed pixels with ScreenCaptureKit, requesting 120 Hz capture on a 60 Hz display. These are captured-response measurements, not physical display latency.

Six alternating Apple-mode/Screen Sharing pairs ran one client at a time, with 16 trials per action per round. Scroll alternated six lines down and up, typing alternated one A and Delete, and menu trials opened TextEdit's File menu and closed it with Escape. The pointer stayed outside the typing region. All 576 planned inputs produced a response. Each insertion shifted the watched line by one cell and each deletion restored it. Every menu remained open for its planned Escape. Independent host process-log checks found no external native-test activity during any pair. No pair or performed observation was replaced or excluded.

The primary estimate is the median of six round medians. Scroll pools both directions; typing measures insertion and menu measures opening. Gaps are Apple mode minus Screen Sharing, in milliseconds.

| Action | Apple mode | Screen Sharing | Gap | 95% paired-cluster interval for gap |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Scroll | 67.7 | 64.4 | +3.3 | [-1.4, +9.8] |
| Type | 58.3 | 64.1 | -5.8 | [-9.5, -1.7] |
| Open menu | 127.8 | 119.4 | +8.4 | [+6.3, +14.8] |

All three observed primary gaps meet the 10 ms point-estimate rule. The menu interval extends beyond 10 ms, so the experiment does not establish that its gap is within 10 ms with 95% confidence. Pooling all menu trials instead gives a 12.4 ms median gap with interval [9.5, 15.6]; that is a different estimate from the prespecified median of round medians.

Trial-level interquartile ranges and confidence intervals replace the original ordering of six observed round standard deviations, as agreed for this series. Each action/direction cell has 48 observations per client.

| Action/direction | IQR Apple / Screen Sharing | IQR gap | 95% paired-cluster interval |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Scroll down | 10.5 / 13.1 | -2.6 | [-8.7, -0.2] |
| Scroll up | 12.5 / 14.4 | -2.0 | [-8.4, +4.3] |
| Insert | 15.6 / 9.4 | +6.2 | [+1.4, +9.1] |
| Delete | 13.4 / 14.0 | -0.6 | [-6.6, +7.4] |
| Open menu | 6.6 / 12.6 | -6.0 | [-11.3, +1.3] |
| Close menu | 15.2 / 14.4 | +0.8 | [-5.8, +10.6] |

Typing insertion has a wider observed IQR in Remora. The prespecified global one-sided spread test gives 19/64 = 0.2969 by swapping whole paired rounds jointly across all six cells. Non-rejection does not establish equal spread or equivalence. The six-round population standard deviations, reported descriptively as Apple / Screen Sharing, are 2.92 / 2.79 ms for scroll, 3.05 / 2.55 for typing, and 3.19 / 2.43 for opening a menu. Confidence intervals use 20,000 paired-cluster bootstrap draws and only six paired clusters. Fixed client order, drift and the small number of clusters limit their interpretation.

The [numeric observations, method, environment audit and reproducer](../../Tools/vnc/benchmarks/2026-11-13/README.md) contain all 576 observations and the complete analysis. Earlier G, H, J and K runs are retained separately and are not pooled into these results. H stopped after a Screen Sharing menu opened and closed before Escape; its cause remains unknown. J stopped on a missing typed glyph, and K stopped on a menu-opening timeout. Host logs match those two Remora incidents and K's earlier menu closures to unrelated native AppKit tests that created key panels on the served Mac. No trace identifies the exact input hop in either incident. This series used a process-log validity rule fixed before collection and encountered no such test run. It does not establish general input reliability.

A separate prospective control compared Apple mode, standard VNC and Screen Sharing with the same 1200 ms quiet period and 8-second settling deadline. It recorded both first changed pixels and the first frame matching the eventual watched region, ignoring only the fixed blinking-caret box for settling and completion matching. Completion uses sampled luminance differences above 48 and the original frame timestamp; it does not add the quiet period. The first-response search and its three-second deadline stayed unchanged. These single-round controls are descriptive and are not pooled into the six-pair analysis.

The table gives first-change / watched-region-completion medians in milliseconds. Scroll uses both directions; the other rows have eight observations per client, except standard-mode menu rows as noted below.

| Action | Apple first / complete | Screen Sharing first / complete | Standard first / complete |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Scroll | 70.0 / 96.4 | 74.8 / 81.9 | 614.3 / 664.7 |
| Insert | 67.8 / 67.8 | 65.2 / 65.2 | 62.2 / 62.2 |
| Delete | 70.0 / 70.0 | 61.4 / 61.4 | 61.6 / 61.6 |
| Open menu | 127.0 / 127.0 | 122.1 / 135.8 | 1124.3 / 1513.2 |
| Close menu | 100.9 / 170.5 | 105.7 / 170.9 | 130.1 / 314.0 |

Apple mode and Screen Sharing each completed all 48 control inputs. Standard mode completed scroll and typing, then its eighth menu opening exceeded the three-second response search. A later capture showed the open menu. The table's standard-mode menu medians therefore condition on seven observed openings and seven closings; one performed opening timed out and the final planned closing was not attempted. The timeout and stopped round are retained, without replacement or imputation. In this control, Apple mode was faster for scrolling and menus; single-key typing was comparable and does not show an Apple-mode advantage.

An earlier standard-mode attempt with the original 400 ms quiet rule stopped when a partial text repaint failed the restoration guard. A later capture showed the restored text. That attempt remains separate. The longer-quiet control was fixed before collecting any of its three client rounds. [Control observations and method](../../Tools/vnc/benchmarks/2026-11-13/COMPLETION-METHOD.txt) retain both metrics, the timeout, sample counts and source hashes.


The decoder and image-quality settings are unchanged. The 303-second editing workload below ran on `36e595f`; later changes preserve window presentation demand and recover a startup timeout. In the earlier 2026-11-08 comparison, Escape in Preview's empty search field left the focus ring visible in both Remora and Screen Sharing; that behavior came from Preview.

## Connection reliability

On 2026-11-12 a signed development build on macOS 27.0.1 connected to a MacBook Pro M3 Pro running macOS 26.6.2 over LAN. A final run on `a9a3584` completed 100 consecutive Apple-mode connections, each returning a nonblack 3024x1964 picture. Every attempt saved a PNG, independently decoded its pixels and recorded its SHA-256 before closing the session. This run needed no recovery handshake. An earlier build also passed 100 consecutive connections, plus three connections that each followed 180 seconds with no VNC client connected. The host used its existing display policy on AC power. Final receipts and images are under `.snap/benchmark/connects-recovery/`; earlier evidence is under `.snap/benchmark/connects-final/` and `.snap/benchmark/connects-idle/`.

Before the recovery fix, one of 112 authenticated connections to the same host received no ServerInit. The host was awake and unlocked. Remora's summary read `native_error=6 phase=18 last_success=17 failure=10`: ARD authentication succeeded and ClientInit was written, but no ServerInit byte arrived before the 10-second read deadline. The host's log and `screensharingd` disassembly identify a lost wakeup in macOS 26.6.2 (25G83). Its authentication thread wakes the server loop before adding the authenticated socket to the descriptor set. The loop can then wait indefinitely without that socket. In the failed connection the log order was reversed from all 111 successful connections, and the server read the waiting ClientInit only when another client connected 224.7 seconds later. macOS 27.0.1 (26A434) adds the socket before sending the wakeup. Nine other first connections to newly started daemons succeeded, so daemon startup or idle time alone does not explain the stall. Logs, analysis and disassembly extracts are under `.snap/serverinit-timeout/`.

Remora recovers from exactly this state once per session. When the Apple profile has selected ARD, the server has accepted authentication, ClientInit has been written, and the ServerInit read reaches its deadline without receiving a byte, the bridge reports error 11. The session worker then frees that native context, with its socket, decoder state and ARD key. It opens one new context to the same endpoint with the same profile and the same credentials. A password typed for the first transport is reused for the second and then dropped. Rejected authentication, cancellation, EOF, a partial ServerInit and standard mode are never retried, and no other security type is tried. The existing 20-second connection deadline covers both transports. Each transport writes its own handshake summary under the same attempt UUID, and the first keeps `native_error=11` with its phase and failure numbers. `appleWithheldServerInitRecoversOnceOnAFreshTransport` covers the recovery against the independent loopback peer. The stall cannot be forced on a real host. The one real-host observation is the manual reconnect 224.7 seconds later, which succeeded while the stalled viewer was still registered.

A 303-second TextEdit workload completed 100 paired typing/deleting, scrolling and File-menu cycles with live frames throughout. Periodic PNGs and independently decoded movie frames showed no visible decoding errors. A static first-line region matched the initial capture exactly after the workload, and the generated document's saved bytes were unchanged. Evidence is under `.snap/apple-editing/run-20261112T133657Z-db7fdf/`.
